title: Endometriosis Affects 190 Million Women. Science Is Finally Catching Up.
excerpt: A landmark genetic study and new diagnostic tools are reshaping the understanding of a disease that has been chronically underfunded and dismissed for decades.
body:
• Endometriosis affects approximately 190 million women worldwide, causing severe symptoms like pelvic pain and infertility.
  • Recent research indicates that endometriosis is a systemic disease, not just a reproductive health issue.
  • A groundbreaking genetic study identified 80 genomic regions linked to endometriosis, revealing potential drug candidates for treatment.
  • New findings confirm numerous symptoms reported by patients, which have often been dismissed by healthcare providers.

Endometriosis — a chronic inflammatory disease where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus — affects roughly one in ten women of reproductive age. That translates to approximately 190 million people worldwide living with a condition that can cause debilitating pelvic pain, heavy menstrual bleeding, infertility, and organ damage. Yet despite its prevalence, endometriosis remains under-researched and frequently misdiagnosed.

A growing body of scientific evidence is now revealing that endometriosis is far more than a reproductive health issue — it is a systemic disease with consequences the medical establishment has only begun to reckon with.

A Genetic Map, Decades Overdue

In April 2026, researchers at Yale University and institutions across Europe published the largest genetic study of endometriosis to date in Nature Genetics. The team analyzed genomes from more than 1.4 million women, including over 105,000 confirmed cases, and identified 80 genomic regions associated with endometriosis risk — 37 of which had never been previously described.

"This research was a collaborative effort involving investigators with diverse expertise to translate the discovery power of several major biobanks into actionable findings that can improve the care of women affected by endometriosis."

— Dr. Renato Polimanti, Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Yale School of Medicine

The study found genetic overlap between endometriosis and adenomyosis, a related condition, and identified potential drug candidates already approved for other diseases. Lead author Dr. Dora Koller of the Sant Pau Research Institute noted that basic research in endometriosis "has arrived later than in other areas, which has limited understanding of the disease for years."

Hundreds of Hidden Symptoms

Perhaps the most striking recent finding is the scientific confirmation of symptoms that patients reported for years but doctors dismissed. A study at UCSF used electronic health records from nearly 40,000 patients across six university health systems and found that women with endometriosis suffered from several hundred distinct symptoms and conditions beyond the expected gynecological ones — including asthma, autoimmune diseases, migraines, gastroesophageal reflux, and chronic fatigue.

"The inflammatory process that is endometriosis can truly affect every single organ system," said Dr. Megan Wasson, a minimally invasive gynecologic surgeon at the Mayo Clinic, who has removed endometrial lesions from patients' lungs, bowels, spleen, and even the pericardial sac surrounding the heart, according to National Geographic.

A separate study from the University Hospital Zurich found that women with endometriosis were more than twice as likely to report debilitating fatigue — even after accounting for factors like pain, insomnia, and depression.

The Funding Gap

The underfunding of endometriosis research has been stark. Between 2010 and 2024, the NIH spent an average of $14.5 million annually on the disease — 0.039% of its budget — according to data compiled by Science. In 2024, that worked out to approximately $3 per woman with endometriosis, compared to $90 per man with prostate cancer and $170 per woman with breast cancer.

"Research on endometriosis is so far behind because it affects women. And it doesn't kill you."

— Dr. Katie Burns, Pathobiologist, University of Cincinnati

Signs of change are emerging. The Gates Foundation has committed $2.5 billion to women's health research globally by 2030, with endometriosis as a priority. In April 2026, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory opened the Seckin Endometriosis Research Center with $20 million in private funding. At MIT, Prof. Linda Griffith is leading what she calls a "moon shot for menstruation science."

From Labs to Living Rooms

More than a dozen biotech companies are developing screening tools using saliva, blood, or menstrual blood to detect biomarkers linked to endometriosis. A proof-of-concept home test at Penn State works like a pregnancy test using menstrual blood. Another approach uses AI and MRI imaging for noninvasive diagnosis.

These tools could dramatically reduce the diagnostic delay, which currently averages seven years. "To have years of pain and not know why — to be dismissed, as many have, being told that severe menstrual cramps are normal or that it's all in their head — it's very disempowering," Dr. Linda Giudice, a reproductive endocrinologist at UCSF, told National Geographic.

As genetic insights translate into drug candidates and new researchers flock to the field — the 2026 World Congress on Endometriosis in Sydney drew record participation — the disease appears to be at an inflection point. The challenge now is converting laboratory momentum into real-world improvements for the millions of women still managing their condition with painkillers and birth control pills, often after years of being told their pain is normal.
image_caption: Endometriosis affects an estimated 190 million women worldwide. New diagnostic tools and treatments are finally bringing the condition out of the shadows.
nri_angle: Endometriosis research breakthroughs and funding shifts could improve care access for the global Indian diaspora, where cultural stigma around menstrual health often compounds diagnostic delays.
